author: Arman Rahman
title: Madison Common Council approves incentivizing downtown developers to create more affordable student housing
text: Madison Live updates all day, breaking news as it happens and weather every 10 minutes Resize:  Reporter  MADISON, Wis. — Madison’s Common Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to make downtown housing more affordable for college students. The original Affordable Housing Height Incentive was adopted last year, but because students pay for housing with loans, grants, and assistance from their families, they aren’t eligible for most traditional housing programs. The city had to change the downtown zoning to work with the University of Wisconsin-Madison to ensure students who need it can get more affordable units. “The student housing market is crazy,” Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said Wednesday. Although it’s called the “height” incentive, Zoning Administrator Katie Bannon said, “It’s a little bit confusing.” “It’s whether they can put more stories within the box of the maximum height in feet,” she said. Bannon said the idea is that if there’s an incentive to build more units, then the developer and city can agree to reserve bedrooms for students from low- to moderate-income families referred by the university. “The Community Development Division within the city will manage the program and be able to adjust, on a project-by-project basis and year-by-year basis, what those rents should be to be affordable,” she said. The zoning change comes after a study published August 26, 2024, commissioned by the city and UW-Madison, found that the average rent for rentals near the UW campus is $1,273 per bed per month. Newer or renovated buildings average $1,575 per bed per month, and those within a mile of campus average $1,746 per unit. “The biggest thing that we keep hearing from students is that they literally just want a place to live that is decent and affordable to them,” District 2 Alder Juliana Bennett, who was part of getting the study done, said. “They just literally need a place to lay their head at night so that they can get up in the morning and go do their studies.” On-campus, the study found there’s less room. Residence halls maintained an occupancy rate of 104% from 2010 to 2023, and rentals near the UW campus have a 98% occupancy rate. “When we don’t provide student housing, that means those students are out there looking for housing a mile, two miles away from campus, even more living out in residential areas, taking away housing that probably is better suited for multi-family, families with children,” Bennett said. Bennett said the zoning change the Common Council approved was “tremendous,” but there’s still more work to be done. “I would love to see us looking to increase our zoning standards just outside of campus areas like the near West Side or around Regent Street, which are prime areas for student activities and student development,” she said. Meanwhile, the mayor hopes the incentive can have a ripple effect on the housing market throughout the city. “It’s all about supply and demand, and if we can increase the supply of housing of all types, we’re already seeing that rents are starting to moderate a little bit, and we hope to see even more of that as our vacancy rate goes up,” she said. ​COPYRIGHT 2024 BY CHANNEL 3000.
